header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT AT LAHORE
Additional District Judge, Sialkot and others
J U D G M E N T
body: Date of Hearing 17.11.2026 For Petitioner(s): M/s Shamshad Ahmad Bajwa, Malik Ali, Ahmad Raza Bajwa and Ch. Umar Farooq, Advocates.
For respondent(s): Nemo for respondents No.2 & 3, who were already proceeded against ex parte vide order dated 27.10.2026.
M/s M. Usman Rafaqat and Muhammad Umar Iqbal, Advocates for respondents No.4 to 6.

HASSAN NAWAZ MAKHDOOM, J.- Through this constitutional petition, the petitioners, who were arrayed as defendants No.5 to 9 in the original suit, have called in question the legality and propriety of order dated 16.03.2017, passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Sialkot, whereby the civil revision preferred by respondents No.2 and 3/plaintiffs was accepted by setting aside order dated 09.03.2016 of the learned Trial Court and their application under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (the “C.P.C.”) seeking amendment of the plaint was allowed.

2. Briefly stated, the controversy arises out of two competing agreements to sell concerning agricultural land situated in District Sialkot. Muhammad Iqbal, predecessor-in-interest of the petitioners, instituted a suit for specific performance on 23.07.1996 on the basis of an agreement dated 09.09.1994, which was decreed on 22.12.1996, followed by execution of a sale deed through Court on 01.10.2000. Meanwhile, respondents No.2 and 3 had instituted a separate suit for specific performance on 12.05.1996, relying upon an agreement dated 04.01.1995. During its pendency, they moved an application for amendment of the plaint and impleadment of Muhammad Iqbal, WP No.14169 of 2017 2 whereupon the learned Trial Court, vide order dated 13.06.2001, permitted impleadment of his legal heirs, i.e., the present petitioners. However, in the amended plaint filed on 09.07.2001, the said respondents incorporated paragraph No.5 and its subparagraphs, pleading fraud and collusion in obtaining the aforesaid decree and consequential sale deed. They also challenged the decree through an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., filed on 07.07.2003, which was dismissed as withdrawn on 28.09.2005. Subsequently, upon objection raised by the petitioners, the learned Trial Court, vide order dated 30.01.2015, directed deletion of the disputed averments from the amended plaint, observing that its incorporation was beyond the scope of the earlier order dated 13.06.2001, which was confined to impleadment of the legal heirs of Muhammad Iqbal. The review application against the said order was dismissed on 27.10.2015, which was never challenged any further. Thereafter, respondents No.2 and 3 again sought substantially the same amendment through an application dated 10.11.2015 under Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., which was dismissed by the learned Trial Court on 09.03.2016. However, the learned Revisional Court, vide impugned order dated 16.03.2017, set aside the said order and allowed the application for amendment of the plaint, primarily on the premise that procedural provisions governing amendment of pleadings warrant liberal interpretation to facilitate adjudication of the real controversy between the parties. Hence, this writ petition.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that the learned Revisional Court failed to appreciate the binding effect of the earlier judicial orders, particularly those dated 30.01.2015 and 27.10.2015, whereby the proposed amendment had already been disallowed and the attempt to secure its restoration through review also remained unsuccessful. It is maintained that the subsequent application under Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., was nothing, but an attempt to circumvent those orders and revive a controversy, which had attained finality. Learned counsel further submits that the respondents, having withdrawn their application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., could not employ the procedural device of amendment of pleadings to indirectly assail the decree and sale deed obtained by the petitioners’ predecessor-in-interest. According to learned counsel, the learned Trial Court had exercised its jurisdiction lawfully and judiciously, whereas the Revisional Court, WP No.14169 of 2017 3 without identifying any jurisdictional defect or material irregularity, substituted its own discretion for that of the Trial Court.

4. It is pertinent to mention that respondents No.2 and 3, being the plaintiffs in the original suit and contesting party herein, failed to enter appearance and were accordingly proceeded against ex parte vide order dated 27.10.2026. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of respondents No.4 to 6, who were arrayed as defendants No.1 to 3 in the original suit and are pro forma respondents in these proceedings, has expressly stated that they have no objection, if the instant petition is accepted and the impugned revisional order is set aside. Be that as it may, neither the absence of the contesting respondents nor the concession made on behalf of the pro forma respondents can furnish a legal basis for interference with a judicial order. The matter, therefore, requires determination on its own merits in accordance with law.

6. The pivotal question requiring determination is whether an amendment of the plaint, substantially identical to one previously disallowed through a judicial order which had attained finality, could subsequently be permitted under Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., and whether the learned Revisional Court was justified in interfering with the refusal of such amendment by the learned Trial Court. In this context, it may be observed that although Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., confers wide discretion upon a Court to permit amendment of pleadings at any stage of the proceedings for determining the real controversy between the parties, such discretion is neither unbridled nor exercisable in disregard of earlier judicial determinations. The provision, being procedural and remedial in nature, undoubtedly warrants liberal construction to advance the cause of substantial justice; however, the expression “at any stage of the proceedings” cannot be stretched to confer an indefeasible right upon a litigant to repeatedly seek substantially the same amendment which has already been declined through an order attaining finality. The discretion vested in the Court must, therefore, be exercised judiciously, keeping in view the bona fides of the applicant, the nature and necessity of the proposed amendment, the prejudice likely to be caused to the opposite party and, above all, the sanctity and finality of earlier judicial orders. WP No.14169 of 2017 4 7. In this context, reliance is placed on the judgment reported as Muhammad Arif Tarar and another v. Matloob Ahmad Warraich and others (PLD 2025 SC 691), wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, while examining the scope and application of Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., held that although amendment of pleadings may be allowed at any stage of the proceedings to facilitate determination of the real controversy between the parties, such discretion is neither absolute nor unrestricted. Its exercise must be guided by sound judicial principles, particularly the bona fides of the applicant, the nature of the proposed amendment, the explanation for delay and the prejudice likely to be caused to the opposite party. Further reference is also made to Abaid Ullah Malik v. Additional District Judge, Mianwali and others (PLD 2013 SC 239), wherein the limitations governing amendment of pleadings were explained, particularly where the proposed amendment changes the nature of the controversy, is actuated by mala fides, prejudices the rights of the adversary or seeks to overcome the effect of earlier judicial determinations. The Hon’ble Supreme Court further laid down the principles enunciated in Muhammad Akram and another v. Altaf Ahmad (PLD 2003 SC 688), Mst. Noor Khatoon through Legal Heirs and another v. Muhammad Shafi (2003 SCMR 542) and Mst. Ghulam Bibi and others v. Sarsa Khan and others (PLD 1985 SC 345), underscoring the significance of unexplained delay, want of due diligence and prejudice to the opposite party in determining whether an amendment ought to be permitted. The ratio decidendi of Muhammad Arif Tarar’s case (supra) is particularly relevant to the controversy in hand, as the Hon’ble Supreme Court upheld the judgment of this Court whereby the revisional order allowing amendment of the plaint had been set aside, thereby reaffirming that the liberal approach contemplated by Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., must remain subject to the settled limitations governing the exercise of judicial discretion.

8. The facts and circumstances of the present case, when examined in light of the aforesaid principles, reveal that the learned Revisional Court failed to appreciate a material aspect of the controversy, e.g., that the order dated 13.06.2001, passed by the learned Trial Court, was confined to impleadment of the legal heirs of Muhammad Iqbal and did not authorize incorporation of averments challenging the decree dated 22.12.1996 and the consequential sale deed. The subsequent inclusion of WP No.14169 of 2017 5 paragraph No.5 and its subparagraphs in the amended plaint was, therefore, objected to by the petitioners, whereupon the learned Trial Court, vide order dated 30.01.2015, directed deletion of the said averments. The respondents’ attempt to seek reconsideration of that order through review also proved unsuccessful on 27.10.2015. Both orders, having remained unchallenged before any higher forum, attained finality and continued to bind the parties to the extent of the matters determined therein. It is a settled principle of law that judicial orders passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction, unless varied or set aside in accordance with law, cannot be circumvented through successive applications seeking substantially identical relief. The principle of finality attached to a judicial order further demands that a question once distinctly raised and judicially determined should not ordinarily be reopened in the same proceedings in the absence of any material change in circumstances or legally sustainable fresh ground, notwithstanding that the strict doctrine of res judicata may not invariably be attracted to every interlocutory order. In the instant case, the subsequent application under Order VI Rule 17, C.P.C., neither disclosed any such change nor furnished an independent basis for reconsideration of the earlier determination. The learned Revisional Court, therefore, fell into material error in permitting reintroduction of the very averments, which had already been ordered to be deleted, thereby unsettling judicial orders that had attained finality and allowing the respondents to achieve indirectly what they had failed to secure through the remedies previously availed of.

9. It is equally significant that the application dated 10.11.2015 neither disclosed any subsequent event nor introduced any newly discovered material fact warranting reconsideration of the earlier determination; rather, it sought restoration of the very averments, which had already been ordered to be deleted. The record further reveals that respondents No.2 and 3 were fully aware of the decree dated 22.12.1996 and the consequential sale deed, having themselves invoked the statutory remedy under Section 12(2), C.P.C., through an application dated 07.07.2003, alleging fraud and misrepresentation, which was subsequently dismissed as withdrawn on 28.09.2005. The respondents had earlier filed application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., but subsequently withdrew the same. The mere withdrawal of those WP No.14169 of 2017 6 proceedings, without adjudication on merits, could not justify reintroduction of substantially identical averments through amendment of the plaint, particularly when no fresh factual or legal grounds were available to warrant such a course. Moreover, the respondents had already been refused permission to include the same averments in the plaint through earlier judicial orders, which having not been assailed any further, had attained finality. They could not, therefore, seek the same relief again without any valid justification. The substance of the relief sought, rather than the form or nomenclature of the application, is decisive in determining its legal effect. Consequently, the learned Trial Court rightly declined to entertain the successive application, which was essentially an attempt to reopen a controversy already determined through orders that had attained finality.

10. The learned Revisional Court appears to have proceeded primarily on the general principle that amendment of pleadings should be liberally allowed to facilitate adjudication of the real controversy between the parties, without appreciating that such discretion cannot be exercised to unsettle earlier judicial determinations, which have attained finality. The distinction between an amendment sought to clarify or complete an existing pleading and a successive application intended to circumvent earlier judicial orders was thus overlooked. The application dated 10.11.2015 was filed almost nineteen years after institution of the suit in 1996, although the respondents were well aware of the relevant facts and had already pursued the available legal remedies. The prolonged delay and repeated applications seeking the same relief raised serious doubts about the bona fides of the respondents, particularly as the proposed amendment was intended to question the validity of an existing decree and the sale deed executed in pursuance thereof. The principles declared by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Muhammad Arif Tarar’s case (supra) are instructive in this regard. Furthermore, the scope of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, C.P.C., is limited to examining the legality and jurisdictional correctness of orders passed by subordinate Courts. Such jurisdiction can be exercised only where the subordinate Court has assumed jurisdiction not vested in it by law, failed to exercise jurisdiction lawfully vested in it, or acted illegally or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction. It does not empower the Revisional Court to substitute its own opinion or discretion WP No.14169 of 2017 7 merely because a different view of the matter is possible, particularly where the order under challenge is based on sound judicial reasoning and relevant considerations.

11. The impugned order dated 16.03.2017, therefore, cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set aside, whereas the order dated 09.03.2016, passed by the learned Trial Court, deserves to be restored.

12. For the foregoing reasons, the instant writ petition is allowed. Consequently, the impugned order dated 16.03.2017, passed by the learned Revisional Court, is set aside, and the order dated 09.03.2016 of the learned Trial Court is restored. The learned Trial Court shall proceed with the pending suit expeditiously, in accordance with law, uninfluenced by any observations made hereinabove, which are confined to the controversy decided through this judgment.
Judge Announced/dictated on 17.11.2026 and signed on 20.11.2026.
Tahir Noor Muhammad Sarwar and others v. Hashmal Khan and others (PLD 2022 SC 13).
